title: Implement the union-find (disjoint set) data structure supporting find and union, with path compression and union by rank, and explain its near-constant time complexity.
shortTitle: Implement Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) with Path Compression and Union by Rank

s1_definition.profdef: Union-find, also called disjoint set union, maintains a collection of disjoint sets and supports two operations: find, which returns a representative identifying the set an element belongs to, and union, which merges the sets of two elements. With two optimisations, path compression during find and union by rank or size during union, both operations run in near-constant amortised time, specifically the inverse Ackermann function, which is at most four for any practical input.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India groups accounts into families that share a common fraud profile. Each account points to another account it trusts as its "head of family," and the true head points to itself. To find which family an account belongs to, you follow the chain of heads until you reach the one pointing to itself. To merge two families you make one family's head point to the other's. Path compression means that while walking up the chain you re-point everyone directly to the top head, so next time the lookup is instant. Union by rank means you always attach the shorter family tree under the taller one, keeping chains short.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each element points toward a set representative; find walks to the root with path compression, union links roots by rank, giving near-constant amortised time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Union-find, also called disjoint set union, maintains a collection of disjoint sets and supports two operations: find, which returns a representative identifying the set an element belongs to, and union, which merges the sets of two elements. With two optimisations, path compression during find and union by rank or size during union, both operations run in near-constant amortised time, specifically the inverse Ackermann function, which is at most four for any practical input.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India groups accounts into families that share a common fraud profile. Each account points to another account it trusts as its "head of family," and the true head points to itself. To find which family an account belongs to, you follow the chain of heads until you reach the one pointing to itself. To merge two families you make one family's head point to the other's. Path compression means that while walking up the chain you re-point everyone directly to the top head, so next time the lookup is instant. Union by rank means you always attach the shorter family tree under the taller one, keeping chains short.

**One line to remember:** Each element points toward a set representative; find walks to the root with path compression, union links roots by rank, giving near-constant amortised time.

sections.s2_technical:
The structure is backed by a parent array where `parent[i]` is the element that i points to, and initially every element is its own parent, meaning every element is its own singleton set. The representative of a set is the root, the element that points to itself. Two elements are in the same set exactly when they have the same root.

Find follows parent links until it reaches the root. The path-compression optimisation makes find also flatten the tree: after finding the root, you re-point every node on the path directly to the root, so future finds are shorter. The clean recursive form is `if (parent[x] != x) parent[x] = find(parent[x]); return parent[x];`, which sets each node's parent to the root as the recursion unwinds. This is the single most important optimisation.

Union first finds the roots of both elements; if they are already equal, the elements are in the same set and nothing happens. Otherwise you link one root under the other. Union by rank attaches the tree with the smaller rank, an upper bound on height, under the one with larger rank, and increments rank only when two equal-rank trees merge. Union by size is a common equivalent that attaches the smaller set under the larger. Both keep trees shallow so that even without compression, chains stay short. Together with path compression, the amortised cost per operation is the inverse Ackermann function, which is effectively constant.

A senior-level nuance is where this shines: detecting cycles while building a graph, Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm, grouping connected components, and dynamic connectivity queries. In banking it is perfect for grouping accounts into fraud rings or clustering transactions that are transitively linked. The structure is not easily decremental, meaning you cannot efficiently split a set once merged, so it suits problems where sets only ever grow.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's fraud team discovers links between accounts, for example two accounts that shared a device or transferred money, and needs to group all transitively linked accounts into the same fraud ring. As new links are found, previously separate rings must merge. This is exactly union-find, because linking two accounts should merge their whole groups.

Problem 2 — The team constantly asks "are these two accounts already in the same ring?" at high volume while links keep arriving, so both the merge and the same-group check must be near-constant time even as rings grow large. Path compression and union by rank deliver that.

In our mini-project we build an `AccountGroups` union-find over integer account indices. The demo links several accounts, checks whether two are connected before and after a linking merges their groups, and logs the group representatives.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: five accounts zero through four, then unions of zero-one, two-three, a connectivity check, a union of one-two, and a final check and count.

Step 1: Initialise. Each account is its own parent, so there are five separate sets. The count is five.

Step 2: Union zero and one. Their roots are zero and one, different and equal rank, so we attach one under zero and bump zero's rank. Now zero and one form one set, and the count drops to four.

Step 3: Union two and three. Similarly, three attaches under two, forming a set, count drops to three. Accounts four is still alone.

Step 4: Check connected zero and three. Find zero gives root zero, find three gives root two. The roots differ, so they are in different sets and the answer is false.

Step 5: Union one and two. Find one gives root zero, find two gives root two. Different roots, equal ranks, so two attaches under zero and zero's rank bumps. Now zero, one, two, three are all in one set. The count drops to two, the merged ring plus the lone account four.

Step 6: Check connected zero and three again. Find zero is zero, and find three now walks three to two to zero, root zero, with path compression re-pointing three directly to zero along the way. Both roots are zero, so the answer is true. The count is two.

```
[2026-10-26 23:29:01] INFO    0 and 3 connected? false
[2026-10-26 23:29:01] INFO    0 and 3 connected? true
[2026-10-26 23:29:01] INFO    distinct fraud rings: 2
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Union-Find (DSU) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Disjoint Set Union with path compression + union by rank     │
  │  Amortised inverse-Ackermann ≈ O(1) per op                   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: AccountGroups only manages set membership                 │
  │  O: swap rank for size heuristic without changing API         │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │             AccountGroups             │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  - parent: int[]                      │  parent pointer per node
  │  - rank: int[]                        │  tree-height bound
  │  - count: int                         │  number of sets
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + find(x): int                       │  path compression
  │  + union(a, b): void                  │  union by rank
  │  + connected(a, b): boolean           │  find(a)==find(b)
  │  + count(): int                       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      Invariant: root is the set representative (parent[root]==root)

  ── State Diagram: Set lifecycle ─────────────────────────

  [n singletons] ──union──→ [fewer, larger sets] ──union──→ [1 set]
  (sets only merge, never split — monotone decreasing count)

  ── Call Chain (union) ────────────────────────────────────

  1. union(a,b): ra=find(a), rb=find(b)
  2.   ra==rb → return (same set)
  3.   attach lower-rank root under higher; tie → bump rank
  4.   count--
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Union-find, or disjoint set union, maintains a collection of disjoint sets and supports two operations. Find returns a representative that identifies which set an element belongs to, and union merges the sets containing two elements. I back it with a parent array where every element initially points to itself as its own singleton set, and the representative of a set is its root, the element that points to itself. Two elements are in the same set exactly when they share the same root.

The power comes from two optimisations. Path compression happens during find: after I walk up to the root, I re-point every node on that path directly to the root, so future lookups are flat and fast. Union by rank attaches the shorter tree under the taller one and only bumps the rank when two equal-height trees merge, which keeps the trees shallow. Together these make both operations run in the inverse Ackermann time, which is effectively constant, at most four for any input you will ever see in practice.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the fraud system to group accounts into rings. When the team discovers a link between two accounts, such as a shared device or a money transfer, I union them, which merges their entire groups, and when they ask whether two accounts are already in the same ring, I check whether find returns the same root. Both operations stay near-constant even as rings grow large, which matters because links arrive continuously and the console queries connectivity at high volume.

The senior-level point I make is that union-find is the backbone of several classic algorithms: detecting cycles while building a graph, Kruskal's minimum spanning tree, and counting connected components. I also note its one limitation, that it is not easily decremental, meaning you cannot efficiently split a set once it has merged, so it fits problems where sets only ever grow, which is exactly the case for accumulating fraud links.
